## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324)4 Discussion

The objective of this study was to investigate the estimated EAR and RNI in Chinese older people with sarcopenia utilizing, for the first time in this population, the minimally-invasive IAAO technique. Our data revealed that the protein EAR and RNI of older people with sarcopenia to be 1.21 and 1.54 g/(kg·d), respectively. The protein EAR obtained in this study for older adults with sarcopenia does not differ from the estimates in older adults without sarcopenia ([19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B19)). But on the basis of FFM, the current estimated protein requirement for older adults with sarcopenia was 1.74 g/(kg·d), which was significantly higher compared with the estimated protein requirement for older adults without sarcopenia of 1.38 g/(kg·d) ([19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B19)). The results of this study suggest that older adults with sarcopenia may have higher protein requirements than those without sarcopenia.

Multiple factors are involved in the process of muscle mass loss ([31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B31)), of which nutrition, especially protein intake, is one of the most important and modifiable factors ([7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B7)). Protein ingestion stimulates muscle protein synthesis rates and suppresses, likely via insulin, muscle protein breakdown rates ([32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B32)). To preserve muscle mass, adequate amounts of dietary protein should be consumed ([31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B31), [33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B33)).

In vulnerable populations such as older adults, the minimally invasive IAAO technique is more practical and less invasive than nitrogen balancing in determining protein requirements ([30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B30)). In our previous study in 16 Chinese older adults (>65 year) without sarcopenia that used the IAAO technique, the protein EAR and RNI were determined to be 0.94 and 1.36 g/(kg·d), respectively ([19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B19)). In the present study, the protein requirements of older adults with sarcopenia were about 30% higher than those of the studies mentioned above ([14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B14)–[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B16), [18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B18)).

In recent years, some studies recommend that older people should consume 1.2–2.0 g/(kg·d) or more of protein, depending on their health status ([34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B34), [35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B35)). Evidence suggests that higher dietary protein intake is beneficial to older adults in keeping good health, promoting disease recovery and maintaining function ([36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B36)). In a cross-sectional examination of 3,213 community-based middle-aged and older persons (mean age: 60.7 years) in China, it was shown that participants who consumed ≥ 1.68 g/(kg·d) had the lowest risk of having low muscle mass ([37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B37)). A 12-week, double-blind, randomized, controlled study in undernourished prefrail and frail older subjects aged 70–85 years showed that protein intake of 1.5 g/(kg·d) had the most beneficial effect in preventing sarcopenia and frailty compared with protein intakes of 0.8 and 1.2 g/(kg·d) ([38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B38)). These results also support that older adults with sarcopenia need to consume more protein daily. Most older adults with acute or chronic illnesses require 1.2–1.5 g/(kg·d) of dietary protein; those with serious illness or injury or severely malnutrition may require up to 2.0 g/(kg·d) ([36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B36), [39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B39)). Although potential negative consequences of a higher protein have been suggested, namely that a diet higher in protein could lead to renal injury and affect bone health, there is currently no scientific foundation for this in human studies ([10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B10), [40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B40), [41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B41)). However, for patients with sarcopenia combined with renal disease, a reasonable protein intake should be set under the guidance of a clinician, and health education and malnutrition monitoring should be implemented.

The approximation for the RNI can also be calculated from the coefficient of variation (CV) of the protein EAR as recommended in the Institution of Medicine report ([23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B23)). In the present study, the approximate of the RNI using 1.25 times the EAR is 1.51 g/(kg·d). A recent study estimated the inter-individual variability as a CV of ~20% based on seven IAAO studies ([42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B42)). The CV of the protein requirements determined by IAAO technique was wider than the ordinary CV obtained from the nitrogen balance test. The CV-weighted mean of three studies conducted at steady state, among adults or older age without exercise load, was 19.0% ([42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B42)). The use of this CV (19.0%) to infer the protein RNI resulted in the RNI of 1.67 g/(kg·d), which is higher than the 1.54 g/(kg·d) obtained by combining standard deviations. These studies are limited and individual differences in older adults may be large, which requires further data to determine whether a CV of 19% is appropriate.

In this study, we have attempted to remove the F 13 CO 2 values at the test protein dose of 0.1 g/(kg·d) and found essentially no difference in the results from when they were not removed. If a test protein dose such as 2.0 g/(kg·d) is added after the 1.8 g/(kg·d) protein dose, the model fit may be even better. Therefore, we recommend that a test protein dose of 0.3–2.0 g/(kg·d) would be more appropriate for older people with sarcopenia. Apart from this, there was no statistically difference in EAR per kilogram of body weight between the two groups. This lack of statistically differences may be attributed to the insufficient sample size (one of the limitations of this study) and the lower body weight of the older adults with sarcopenia. Further studies are warranted to differentiate between genders and determine the protein requirement in older adults with sarcopenia.

The IAAO technology is controversial ([43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B43)–[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B45)), and has been criticized on methodologic grounds ([45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B45)). The main issues include the selection and intake of the indicated amino acids, and the length of the adaptation period. The criticisms were discussed in the response of Scherbinsky et al. as well as in recent studies ([44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B44), [46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B46), [47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B47)). The design of the IAAO studies requires a range of test amino acid or protein intakes be studied, holding the indicator amino acid intake constant ([30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B30)). Thus, any changes in IAAO are reflective of changes in the test amino acid or protein intakes and inversely associated with protein synthesis. In different protein level diets, the addition of phenylalanine and tyrosine was made to ensure their intakes matched their content in the highest protein level, and this meant that phenylalanine and tyrosine was never limiting for the utilization of the protein in the meals. This was in contrast to most of the other studies where the IAAO technique was used to study protein requirements where the much lower intakes of phenylalanine and tyrosine might have limited protein utilization at high levels of protein intake ([45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11906324#B45)).

In conclusion, our results suggest that the mean EAR of protein in older Chinese adults with sarcopenia is 1.21 (95% CI: 0.95, 1.46) g/(kg·d), and the RNI is 1.54 (95% CI: 1.13, 1.95) g/(kg·d). Older adults with sarcopenia may need higher protein intake than Chinese older adults without sarcopenia. Due to the small sample size in this study as well as the variation between and within-subject, more studies with larger sample sizes and repeated measures trials are needed to evaluate the protein requirements of older people with sarcopenia.

6. Include relevant dates, names, and locations that are crucial to understanding the content.
7. Summarize lengthy explanations while keeping the core message intact.

When handling different types of content:

- For opinion pieces: Maintain the main arguments and supporting points.

args.key_excerpts: The mean estimated average requirement (EAR) and recommended nutrient intake (RNI) of protein for older adults with sarcopenia were 1.21 (95% CI: 0.95, 1.46) and 1.54 (95% CI: 1.13, 1.95) g/(kg·d), respectively., To our knowledge, this is the first study of protein intake in older adults with sarcopenia and indicates that older adults with sarcopenia may require a higher intake of dietary protein., The protein requirement per kilogram of FFM was significantly higher in older adults with sarcopenia than in older adults without sarcopenia (P = 0.0018)., In the present study, the protein requirements of older adults with sarcopenia were about 30% higher than those of the studies mentioned above, Most older adults with acute or chronic illnesses require 1.2–1.5 g/(kg·d) of dietary protein; those with serious illness or injury or severely malnutrition may require up to 2.0 g/(kg·d)
args.summary: This study, published in Frontiers in Nutrition (2025), investigates dietary protein requirements for older adults with sarcopenia using the indicator amino acid oxidation (IAAO) technique. Nine Chinese adults aged 66-81 with sarcopenia (diagnosed per AWGS 2019 criteria) participated, consuming protein intakes ranging from 0.1 to 1.8 g/(kg·d). The estimated average requirement (EAR) for protein was 1.21 g/(kg·d) (95% CI: 0.95-1.46), and the recommended nutrient intake (RNI) was 1.54 g/(kg·d) (95% CI: 1.13-1.95). When expressed per kilogram of fat-free mass (FFM), the protein requirement for sarcopenic adults (1.74 g/(kg·d)) was significantly higher than for healthy older adults (1.38 g/(kg·d), p=0.0018). This is the first study to determine protein requirements specifically in older adults with sarcopenia, suggesting they need higher protein intake than older adults without sarcopenia. The authors recommend a test protein dose range of 0.3-2.0 g/(kg·d) for future studies in this population and note that larger sample sizes are needed.

Volume 7, Number 12, December 2015, pages 926-931

**Nutrition for Sarcopenia**

Hidekatsu Yanai

Department of Internal Medicine, National Center for Global Health and Medicine Kohnodai Hospital, 1-7-1 Kohnodai, Chiba 272-8516, Japan

Manuscript accepted for publication October 12, 2015  
Short title: Nutrition for Sarcopenia  
doi: http://dx.doi.org/10.14740/jocmr2361w

* [Abstract](#s0)
* [Introduction](#s1)
* [The Association Between Energy Intake and the Development of Sarcopenia](#s2)
* [The Association Between Protein Intake and the Development of Sarcopenia](#s3)
* [Clinical Trials to Study Effects of Nutritional Factors on Sarcopenia](#s4)
* [Conclusion](#s5)
* [References](#references)

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| **Abstract** | [▴Top](#top) |

---

Aging-related sarcopenia means that muscle mass, strength, and physical performance tend to decline with age, and malnutrition is associated with sarcopenia. Therefore, nutritional interventions may make an important contribution to prevent the development of sarcopenia. Here I reviewed published articles about the effects of nutritional factors on sarcopenia in elderly people. A growing body of evidence suggests that metabolic factors associated with obesity and diabetes induce the progression of sarcopenia. However, the effectiveness and safety of caloric restriction for sarcopenia remained unclear. Protein intake and physical activity are the main anabolic stimuli for muscle protein synthesis. As optimal dietary protein intake, 1.0 - 1.2 g/kg (body weight)/day with an optimal repartition over each daily meal or 25 - 30 g of high quality protein per meal were recommended to prevent sarcopenia, which was supported by some observational studies. Protein supplementation using cheese and milk protein, essential amino acids, leucine, beta-hydroxy-beta-methylbutyrate and vitamin D has been investigated as a potential supplement to improve muscle quality in sarcopenic elderly people.

**Keywords:** Beta-hydroxy-beta-methylbutyrate; Energy restriction; Leucine; Protein intake; Sarcopenia

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| **Introduction** | [▴Top](#top) |

---

The number of elderly people has been rapidly increasing in Japan. The growing number of elderly people has compelled us to focus on aging-related sarcopenia. Sarcopenia indicates that muscle mass, strength, and physical performance tend to decline with age, therefore sarcopenia becomes increasingly prevalent with age [[1-3](#R01)]. As sarcopenia is a major predictor of frailty, hip fracture, disability and mortality in elderly persons [[1-3](#R01)], the development of effective management to treat it is eagerly awaited. Malnutrition is one of factors which induce sarcopenia [[3](#R03)]. Nutritional interventions may make an important contribution to avenues for prevention of sarcopenia. However, nutritional management for sarcopenia remains largely unknown. Here I reviewed published articles about the effects of nutritional factors on sarcopenia in elderly people.

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| **The Association Between Energy Intake and the Development of Sarcopenia** | [▴Top](#top) |

---

A growing body of evidence suggests that metabolic factors associated with obesity and diabetes induce the progression of sarcopenia [[4](#R04)]. Recently, the age-related change in the body composition such as a combination of excess weight and reduced muscle mass/strength is defined as sarcopenic obesity [[5](#R05)]. Sarcopenic obesity is associated with the upregulation of inflammatory cytokines [[5](#R05)], which further deteriorates sarcopenia [[6](#R06)]. Is energy restriction (ER) effective to prevent obesity/diabetes-related sarcopenia? In the systematic review using 52 studies including exercise (EX), ER, or ER + EX groups, 81% and 39% of the ER and ER + EX groups, respectively, lost over 15% of body weight as fat-free mass (FFM) [[7](#R07)]. Study participants had to have a mean age of ≥ 50 years and mean body mass index (BMI) of ≥ 25 kg/m2. Studies that had very low calorie diets (≤ 800 calories per day) were excluded. This study suggests that EX preserves FFM after moderate ER, and also indicates that ER induces FFM loss even in obese people. Normandin et al identified 19 published papers from 10 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) ranging from 3 to 18 months that reported independent effects of a caloric restriction (CR) on the health benefits in adults with a mean age of ≥ 65 years [[8](#R08)]. They concluded that the risk-to-benefit ratio of CR for the treatment of obesity in elderly adults remains unclear. We should determine the adequate energy intake to prevent or treat sarcopenia by performing further studies in the future.

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| **The Association Between Protein Intake and the Development of Sarcopenia** | [▴Top](#top) |

---

In the cross-sectional study combined five datasets (n = 900), 77% of all participants had lower than recommended protein intake [[9](#R09)], indicating the existence of insufficient protein intake in heterogeneous elderly populations.

Protein intake and physical activity are the main anabolic stimuli for muscle protein synthesis. Aging causes loss of various anabolic signals to muscle that are present in young people [[10](#R10)]. Such “anabolic resistance” is associated with the development of sarcopenia [[10](#R10)]. Amino acids alone stimulate muscle protein synthesis in the elderly. However, mixed nutritional supplementation failed to improve muscle mass. Volpi et al found that the response of muscle protein anabolism to hyperaminoacidemia with endogenous hyperinsulinemia is impaired in healthy elderly people [[11](#R11)].

How much protein should elderly people with anabolic resistance ingest? Rizzoli reported the recommendations for optimal dietary protein intake are daily 1.0 - 1.2 g/kg (body weight) with an optimal repartition over each daily meal to prevent sarcopenia [[12](#R12)]. Paddon-Jones et al proposed a dietary plan that includes 25 - 30 g of high quality protein per meal as dietary protein recommendations for the prevention of sarcopenia [[13](#R13)].

Bopp et al investigated the association between dietary protein intake and loss of lean mass (LM) during a 20-week weight loss intervention in postmenopausal women [[14](#R14)]. Protein intake averaged 0.62 g/kg/day (0.47 - 0.8 g/kg/day). Participants who consumed higher amounts of dietary protein lost less LM; however, these participants (0.8 g/kg/day) also lost LM. These results suggested that an inadequate protein intake may be associated with LM loss, and daily protein intake ≤ 0.8 g/kg was not sufficient to prevent LM loss in postmenopausal women.

Houston et al studied to determine the association between dietary protein and changes in total LM in elderly, community-dwelling men and women [[15](#R15)]. Energy-adjusted protein intake was associated with 3-year changes in LM. Participants in the highest quintile of protein intake (1.2 g/kg/day) lost approximately 40% less LM than did those in the lowest quintile of protein intake (0.8 g/kg/day).

In Japan, Kobayashi et al examined the association of protein and amino acid intake with frailty among elderly Japanese women [[16](#R16)]. Subjects categorized to the third (69.8 - 76.1 g/day), fourth (76.1 - 84.3 g/day), and fifth quintiles (76.1 - 84.3 g/day) of total protein intake showed significantly lower odds ratios than those to the first quintile (≤ 62.9 g/day).

Recently the study was undertaken to evaluate differences in protein intake in women with or without sarcopenia [[17](#R17)]. Elderly women older than 65 years with sarcopenia (n = 35) and without sarcopenia (n = 165) participated in the study. Muscle mass was significantly higher in women who had protein intake > 1.2 g/kg/day. Protein and energy intake were significant predictors of muscle mass.

These results agreed with the recommendation for protein intake such as 1.0 - 1.2 g/kg/day (daily 60 - 72 g for 60 kg weighted subjects) and 25 - 30 g of high quality protein per meal (daily 75 - 90 g).

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| **Clinical Trials to Study Effects of Nutritional Factors on Sarcopenia** | [▴Top](#top) |

---

Clinical trials to study effects of nutritional factors on sarcopenia were shown in [Table 1](#T1) [[18-36](#R18)]. The adding daily 210 g of ricotta cheese to the habitual diet improved the markers of sarcopenia in subjects without a pronounced loss of skeletal muscle mass [[18](#R18)]. Dietary milk protein supplementation improved physical performance, but did not increase skeletal muscle mass in frail elderly people [[19](#R19)]. Fast-digestive soluble milk protein supplement for 10 days overcame muscle anabolic resistance and improved postprandial muscle protein synthesis in healthy elderly men [[20](#R20)]. In 65 sarcopenic elderly Malays aged 60 - 74 years, there was an increase in FFM (+5.7%) in the EX group after 12 weeks. The highest increments in lower body strength was observed in the protein supplementation group (73.2%) [[21](#R21)].

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| [Table 1.  Click to view](http://www.jocmr.org/tables/jocmr2361wt.htm#outT1) | ***Table 1.** Clinical Trials to Study Effects of Protein, Amino Acids, Leucine, Vitamin D, HMB Intake on Sarcopenia* |

One hundred fifty-five sarcopenic women aged 75 and older were randomly assigned to EX and amino acid supplementation, EX, amino acid supplementation, or health education. EX and amino acid supplementation together was effective in enhancing not only muscle strength, but also combined variables of muscle mass and walking speed in sarcopenic women [[22](#R22)]. Daily ingestion of 15 g essential amino acids (EAA) improved LM and basal muscle protein synthesis in elderly individuals [[23](#R23)]. Ingestion of 8 g of EAA snacks twice a day, significantly increased LM after 6 months and more consistently after 18 months [[24](#R24)]. An oral amino acid supplement improved ambulatory capacity and maximal isometric muscle strength in elderly subjects [[25](#R25)]. Supplementation of the diet with EAA plus arginine also improved LM, strength and physical function compared to baseline values in glucose intolerant elderly individuals [[26](#R26)]. Coker et al recruited and randomized 12 elderly individuals to an 8-week, CR diet utilizing equivalent caloric meal replacements (800 kcal/day): 1) whey protein + EAA meal replacement (EAAMR) or 2) competitive meal replacement (CMR) in conjunction with 400 kcal of solid food that totaled 1,200 kcal/day designed to induce 7% weight loss [[27](#R27)]. Both groups lost about 7% of total body weight. While EAAMR did not promote a significant preservation of LM, the reduction in adipose tissue was greater in EAAMR compared to CMR. These results indicate that quality of protein and energy intake are associated with prevention of sarcopenia.

Aging is associated with changes in the muscle protein metabolism response to a meal, due to alterations in the response to endogenous hormones. The older muscle is still able to respond to amino acids such as leucine, leucine initiates mRNA translation, which is still present in elderly people [[37](#R37)]. Long-term EAA supplementation including excess leucine may be a useful tool for the prevention and treatment of sarcopenia [[37](#R37)]. Beta-hydroxy-beta-methylbutyrate (HMB), a metabolite of the branched-chain amino acid leucine, has been investigated as a potential supplement to improve muscle quality [[38](#R38)].

Bukhari et al performed a single-dose administration (whey protein or novel low-dose leucine-enriched EAA (3 g, 40% leucine)) [[28](#R28)]. However, they did not show the difference in muscle anabolism between whey protein and novel low-dose leucine-enriched EAA by a single-dose administration [[28](#R28)].

Vitamin D has been known to have a role in skeletal muscle health [[39](#R39)]. Further, regular EX is the strategy found to consistently prevent frailty and improve sarcopenia and physical function in elderly adults [[40](#R40)]. Resistance EX training is effective in increasing muscle mass and strength [[40](#R40)].

The supplementation of vitamin D alone provided significant protective effect against the occurrence of sarcopenia and significant increases in muscle strength in postmenopausal women [[29](#R29)]. In a 2 × 2 factorial-design trial, subjects were randomly assigned either to a whole-body vibration (WBV) or a no-training group, receiving either a conventional dose (880 IU/day) or a high dose (1,600 IU/day) of vitamin D [[30](#R30)]. A higher dose of vitamin D did not provide additional musculoskeletal benefit compared with conventional doses.

A protein-enriched diet equivalent to 1.3 g/kg/day achieved through lean red meat is safe and effective for enhancing the effects of progressive resistance training on LM and muscle strength [[31](#R31)]. The 13-week intervention of a vitamin D and leucine-enriched whey protein oral nutritional supplement resulted in improvements in muscle mass and lower-extremity function among sarcopenic elderly adults [[32](#R32)]. A high whey protein-, leucine-, and vitamin D-enriched supplement preserved muscle mass during intentional weight loss in obese elderly adults [[33](#R33)].

HMB supplementation for 2 - 4 weeks could reduce muscle breakdown in bed-ridden elderly nursing home residents receiving tube feeding [[34](#R34)]. Daily supplementation of HMB, arginine, and lysine for 12 weeks beneficially altered measurements of muscle functionality, strength, FFM, and protein synthesis [[35](#R35)]. Consumption of a simple amino acid-related cocktail (HMB, arginine and lysine) increased protein turnover and LM in elderly individuals in a year-long study [[36](#R36)].

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| **Conclusion** | [▴Top](#top) |

---

I reviewed published articles about the effects of nutritional factors on sarcopenia. Epidemiological studies suggested that a low protein intake is associated with sarcopenia. The effectiveness and safety of ER for sarcopenic obesity remains unclear. As optimal dietary protein intake, daily 1.0 - 1.2 g/kg with an optimal repartition over each daily meal or 25 - 30 g of high quality protein per meal were recommended to prevent sarcopenia, which was supported by some observational studies. Cheese and milk protein, EAA, leucine, HMB and vitamin D have been investigated as a potential supplement to improve muscle quality in sarcopenic elderly people. Some studies showed the effectiveness of these nutritional factors for sarcopenia. However, we should consider the appropriate concomitant energy intake, the combination of these factors and the combination with physical activities, to develop a better management for sarcopenia. Further studies, preferably with larger numbers of elderly subjects, will be needed.

**Competing Interests**

The authors declare that they have no competing interests.

This work was funded by a grant from the National Center for Global Health and Medicine (26-112).

args.summary:
This is a scientific review article titled "Nutrition for Sarcopenia" by Hidekatsu Yanai, published in the Journal of Clinical Medicine Research (Vol. 7, No. 12, December 2015, pages 926-931). The review examines the effects of nutritional factors on sarcopenia (aging-related decline in muscle mass, strength, and physical performance) in elderly people.

Key findings include:
- Metabolic factors associated with obesity and diabetes accelerate sarcopenia progression, but the effectiveness and safety of caloric restriction for sarcopenic obesity remains unclear.
- Protein intake and physical activity are the main anabolic stimuli for muscle protein synthesis. Recommended optimal dietary protein intake is 1.0-1.2 g/kg body weight/day with optimal repartition over each daily meal, or 25-30 g of high quality protein per meal.
- Observational studies support these recommendations: participants in the highest quintile of protein intake (1.2 g/kg/day) lost approximately 40% less lean mass than those in the lowest quintile (0.8 g/kg/day).
- Various supplements have been investigated: cheese and milk protein, essential amino acids (EAA), leucine, beta-hydroxy-beta-methylbutyrate (HMB), and vitamin D.
- Clinical trials showed that exercise combined with amino acid supplementation was effective in enhancing muscle strength and mass in sarcopenic women. A vitamin D and leucine-enriched whey protein supplement improved muscle mass and lower-extremity function.
- The author concludes that further studies with larger numbers of elderly subjects are needed, particularly regarding appropriate concomitant energy intake, combination of nutritional factors, and combination with physical activities.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315)Abstract

### Purpose of review

To draw attention to recent work on the role of protein and the amount of protein needed with each meal to preserve skeletal muscle mass in ageing.

### Recent findings

Ageing does not inevitably reduce the anabolic response to a high-quality protein meal. Ingestion of approximately 25–30g of protein per meal maximally stimulates muscle protein synthesis in both young and older individuals. However, muscle protein synthesis is blunted in elderly when protein and carbohydrate are coingested or when the quantity of protein is less than approximately 20g per meal. Supplementing regular mixed-nutrient meals with leucine may also enhance the muscle protein synthetic response in elders.

### Summary

On the basis of recent work, we propose a novel and specific dietary approach to prevent or slow-muscle loss with ageing. Rather than recommending a large, global increase in the recommended dietary allowance (RDA) for protein for all elderly individuals, clinicians should stress the importance of ingesting a sufficient amount of protein with each meal. To maximize muscle protein synthesis while being cognizant of total energy intake, we propose a dietary plan that includes 25–30g of high quality protein per meal.

**Keywords:**aging, leucine, muscle protein synthesis, protein intake, sarcopenia

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315)Introduction

Sarcopenia is a progressive, insidious process characterized by 3–8% reduction in lean muscle mass per decade after the age of 30 years. It is thought to affect 30% of individuals over 60 years of age and more than 50% of those over 80 years [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R1)]. Research continues to focus on the mechanisms contributing to sarcopenia. This has included studies focusing on protein metabolism and cell signaling, voluntary or imposed reductions in physical activity, protein energy malnutrition and reduced anabolic efficiency to protein ingestion [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R2)–[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R4),[5•](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R5)]. Although protein synthesis and ultimately skeletal muscle mass are regulated by a host of factors, the fundamental prerequisite for muscle protein synthesis is dietary derived amino acids. The purpose of this review is to highlight recent research examining the role of protein in the prevention or management of sarcopenia and provide recommendations on the amount of protein needed with each meal to preserve skeletal muscle mass in ageing.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315)Ageing and the skeletal muscle protein synthesis response to feeding

Several studies have examined the acute and chronic effects of protein ingestion/supplementation on muscle protein anabolism in elders and the results have been well documented [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R4),[5•](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R5),[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R6)–[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R8),[9••](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R9),[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R10)]. The majority of studies suggest that a moderate-to-large serving of protein or amino acids increases muscle protein synthesis similarly in both young and elderly [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R6),[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R7),[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R11)–[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R17)]. Conversely, one recent study with a nice mix of signaling and metabolic measures but limited cohort (_n_ = 4 per group) reported that 10 and 20g servings of essential amino acids were unable to stimulate muscle protein synthesis in older individuals to the same level as noted in the young [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R2)].

Historically, the majority of protein metabolism studies have focused on the anabolic response to ingestion of protein or amino acids alone. However, when protein and carbohydrate are coingested, elderly respond with a diminished anabolic response compared with their younger counterparts. Volpi _et al._, [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R18)] demonstrated that after ingestion of an amino acid glucose mixture, muscle protein synthesis increased in the young, but remained unchanged in the elderly. A subsequent study confirmed these results [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R19)]. Although there is no evidence that coingestion of protein and fat negatively or differentially effects protein anabolism in young or elderly [[9••](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R9),[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R20)], it appears that ageing may be associated with reduced anabolic efficiency in response to a carbohydrate-containing mixed nutrient meal. Fortunately, a modest bout of physical activity may be able to sensitize ageing muscle to subsequent nutritional stimuli. We have recently shown that 45min of treadmill walking in older individuals, the evening prior to an hyperinsulinemic–euglycemic clamp, restores the ability of insulin to stimulate muscle protein synthesis [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R4)]. More recently, we demonstrated that ingestion of leucine-enriched essential amino acids stimulates muscle protein synthesis to a similar extent in young and elderly (although the response was delayed in the elderly) during the first 6 hours following exercise [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R21)]. These data provide further supporting evidence that regular physical activity plays an important role in restoring or maintaining the normal protein anabolic response in the skeletal muscle of older individuals.

As mentioned, numerous studies support the notion that ingestion of a sufficient amount of amino acids or protein results in a similar increase in muscle protein synthesis in young and elderly [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R7),[9••](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R9),[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R22)]. However, several recent studies have adopted a more practical approach and sought to examine the ability of protein-rich foods (e.g., milk) to stimulate protein anabolism. Although many of these studies have focused on a younger population [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R23),[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R24)], they are important as they more closely reflect responses to actual dietary practices and hence provide information on how meal choices may influence accrual of muscle mass and ultimately functional capacity. In one study directly comparing young and elderly, Symons _et al._ [[9••](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R9)] reported that a moderate 113g serving of an intact protein (that is, lean beef) contains sufficient amino acids (30g total; ~12g essential amino acids) to increase mixed muscle protein synthesis by 50% in both young and elderly men and women.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315)Should protein intake be increased in the elderly?

The adequacy of the recommended dietary allowance (RDA) for protein has been the subject of renewed debate over the past 12 months [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R25)–[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R30)]. The current recommendation for protein intake for all men and women aged 19 years and older is 0.8g.kg−1.d−1. The recommendations were established by the Institute of Medicine and based on short-duration nitrogen balance studies in young adults [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R31),[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R32)]. Much of the recent commentary has argued that the current RDA for protein, while fulfilling the criteria as the ‘minimal daily average dietary intake level that meets the nutritional requirements of nearly all healthy individuals’, does not promote optimal health or protect elders from sarcopenic muscle loss [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R27),[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R33),[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R34),[35••](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R35)]. Although there is no consensus on the degree to which dietary protein needs change with advancing age, there is general agreement that additional longer term trials with defined health outcomes are needed to firmly establish the optimal protein intake range for various population groups [[35••](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R35)]. Although absolutely necessary, this process is certainly complicated by the host of mechanisms that contributing to sarcopenia. In the following sections, we argue that whereas a modest increase in protein intake beyond 0.8g.kg−1.d−1 may indeed be beneficial for some elders, there is a greater need to specifically examine the dose and distribution of protein across each meal.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315)An adequate amount of protein intake with each meal is essential

Although specialized supplementation with amino acid products may be beneficial or necessary in specific elderly or clinical populations [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R36),[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R37)], the most practical means of promoting skeletal muscle protein anabolism for the majority of older adults is to include a moderate serving of protein of high biological value during each meal. For example, an often-neglected aspect of daily protein intake that directly impacts net protein balance is the distribution of protein across three or more daily meals. For a 75 kg individual, the RDA represents 60g protein/day, or if distributed evenly across three meals, 20 g protein/meal. A 20 g serving of most animal or plant-based proteins contains 5–8 g of essential amino acids, which are primarily responsible for stimulating muscle protein synthesis [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R15)]. This is an important issue because it has been recently shown that ageing is associated with an inability of skeletal muscle to respond to low doses (~7.5 g) of essential amino acids whereas higher doses (10–15 g) are capable of stimulating muscle protein synthesis to a similar extent as the young [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R7),[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R38)].

To examine the effect of protein dose on muscle protein anabolism using a protein-rich food, we recently demonstrated that ingestion of a large single 340 g serving of lean beef (90 g protein) in a cohort of healthy young and elderly individuals does not elicit a greater anabolic response than a serving one-third the size (Symons _et al._ [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R9)], in review). Although this response may be influenced by physical activity (habitual and acute) and body size (lean muscle mass), the data suggests that, despite the additional protein and energy content, ingestion of more than 30 g of protein in a single meal may be an energetically inefficient means of stimulating muscle protein synthesis. Further, a recent study in healthy elders has shown that a large increase in the overall daily protein intake for 10 days did not improve protein anabolism and concerns were expressed over changes in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R10)].

If we accept that 25–30 g of high quality protein (~10 g EAA) is necessary to maximally stimulate skeletal muscle protein synthesis, then it seems reasonable to suggest that ingestion of this amount of high-quality protein at each meal could be a useful strategy to maintain muscle mass in the elderly. In [Fig. 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#F1)[Fig. 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#F1), we provide a pictorial example of the proposed relationship between the amount of protein ingested per meal and the resultant anabolic response. The influence of factors such as physical activity notwithstanding, it is clear that the distribution of protein depicted in [Fig. 1a](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#F1), would result in a greater 24 h net protein balance than the protein distribution pattern depicted in [Fig. 1b](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#F1).

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315)Leucine supplementation to prevent sarcopenia

The rationale for the use of a nutritional supplement to slow or prevent sarcopenic muscle loss is based on the assumption that it will improve net muscle protein synthesis above that afforded by regular meals alone. In addition to this direct anabolic effect, the additional energy/nutrient content of a supplement should not interfere with the normal anabolic response to protein consumed as part of daily meals [[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R39)]. Many attempts have been made to combat muscle and strength loss in elderly via protein or amino acid supplementation see review by Milne _et al._, [[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R40)]. In some cases, protein–energy supplementation has been shown to be effective. However, other trials, particularly those involving acutely ill or frail patient populations, have been unsuccessful (11–13). In some instances protein supplementation increases satiety and simply replaces voluntary ingestion of regular menu items [[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R39),[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R41)]. For others, cost, availability or medical complications such as dysphagia or impaired kidney function may limit the applicability or efficacy of protein supplementation regimens. In such instances, maximizing protein anabolism whereas minimizing the amount or volume of supplementation ingested would be desirable.

Leucine is an insulin secretagogue with well described effects on translation initiation and muscle protein synthesis [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R22),[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R42)–[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R44)]. Notably, leucine is a potent activator of the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) nutrient and energy-sensing signaling pathway, in skeletal muscle. Increased insulin availability increases muscle protein synthesis by enhancing phosphorylation of Akt/PKB (an upstream regulator of mTOR), whereas increased leucine availability promotes the phosphorylation and activation of the downstream effectors of mTOR, 4E-BP1 and S6K1 [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R3),[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R21)]. With increasing age, muscle may become resistant to the stimulatory effects of normal postprandial concentrations of leucine [[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R42)]. Although such a deficit could contribute to reduced muscle protein anabolism and a loss of muscle mass, recent acute studies in both animals [[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R42),[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R45),[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R46)] and humans [[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R47)–[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R49)] suggest that the addition of supplemental leucine to normal mixed nutrient meals may improve or normalize muscle protein synthesis in aging muscle. Specifically, Rieu _et al._ [[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R46)] reported that in older rats, muscle protein synthesis following a normal mixed nutrient meal, was blunted compared with younger animals. However, the addition of supplemental leucine to the meal restored muscle protein synthesis to youthful levels in the older rats [[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R46)]. In a follow-up study in older humans, the addition of leucine to a mixed nutrient meal also resulted in a significant increase in muscle protein synthesis (0.053 ± 0.009%/h vs. 0.083 ± 0.008 %/h, _P_< 0.05) [[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R47)]. Pansarasa _et al._ [[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R50)] recently reported that amino acid supplementation in rats can prevent sarcopenia apparently through increased activation of the mTOR signaling pathway. These new findings are promising for the potential use of added leucine to regular meals in an effort to maximally stimulate muscle protein synthesis in the elderly.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315)Ageing and the interaction of physical activity and protein/nutrient intake

Elderly individuals are at increased risk of being physically incapacitated or placed on bed rest for an extended period. The loss of lean body mass is dramatically increased during inactivity and is driven by a chronic imbalance between muscle protein synthesis and breakdown and facilitated by decreased activation of the mTOR nutrient signaling pathway [[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R51),[52•](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R52),[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R53)]. In recent studies examining changes in protein synthesis and muscle mass in healthy adults subjected to bed rest, older individuals experienced an approximate three-fold greater loss of lean leg muscle mass compared with a cohort of younger individuals confined to bed for 28 days [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R12),[52•](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R52)]. In a medically compromised inpatient population, this could contribute to decreased immune function, impaired wound healing impact and delayed recovery following discharge [[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R54)]. The standard treatment modality for hospitalized elders is weight-bearing exercise [[55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R55),[56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R56)]. Unfortunately, a substantial number of hospitalized or institutionalized elderly are severely limited in their ability to perform any physical activity [[57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315#R57)]. In such instances, protein–energy supplementation represents one of the few viable alternatives.

The benefits of regular resistance exercise in elders have been well described. However, unlike younger individuals, the chronic additive or synergistic effects of combined protein supplementation and resistance exercise on muscle mass and function are less clear (37–39). In a recent study, 36 older men and women performed 12 week of resistance training in association with a lower (0.9 g protein kg−1.d−1) or higher protein (1.2 g protein kg−1.d−1) intake. There was general improvement in all outcome measures (e.g., strength, whole-body protein accretion and reduced fat mass), however, there were no significant differences between the lower-protein groups and higher-protein groups (38). Similarly, using a postexercise supplement, Andrews _et al._ (37) reported that differences in daily protein intake (1.35 vs. 0.72 g protein kg−1.d−1) did not differentially affect lean mass gains following a 12-week resistance exercise program in older men and women (60–69 years). Further studies designed to clarify this apparent age-related difference and identify key mechanistic event are needed.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2760315)Conclusion

Ageing is associated with a reduced ability to stimulate skeletal muscle protein synthesis in response to feeding, insulin, and resistance exercise. We propose a novel and specific dietary approach to. To prevent or slow sarcopenic muscle loss, clinicians should stress the importance of ingesting a sufficient amount of protein with each meal. To maximize muscle protein synthesis whereas being cognizant of total energy intake, we propose a dietary plan that includes 25–30 g of high quality protein per meal.

args.summary:
This article by Paddon-Jones and Rasmussen (2009), published in Current Opinion in Clinical Nutrition and Metabolic Care, reviews the role of dietary protein in preventing sarcopenia (age-related muscle loss). Key findings: 

- Sarcopenia is characterized by a 3-8% reduction in lean muscle mass per decade after age 30, affecting 30% of those over 60 and more than 50% of those over 80.
- Ageing does not inevitably reduce the anabolic response to high-quality protein; ingestion of 25-30g of protein per meal maximally stimulates muscle protein synthesis in both young and older individuals.
- However, muscle protein synthesis is blunted in elderly when protein and carbohydrate are coingested or when protein quantity is less than ~20g per meal.
- The current RDA for protein (0.8g/kg/day for all adults 19+) was based on short-duration nitrogen balance studies in young adults and may not be optimal for preventing sarcopenic muscle loss.
- Supplementing meals with leucine (a potent activator of the mTOR signaling pathway) may enhance muscle protein synthesis in ageing muscle.
- Physical activity (even moderate walking) can sensitize ageing muscle to nutritional stimuli and help restore normal protein anabolic responses.
- The authors propose a practical dietary plan: 25-30g of high-quality protein per meal, distributed evenly across meals, rather than a large global increase in total daily protein intake.

# 健康饮食餐盘 (Chinese – Simplified)

“健康饮食餐盘”由哈佛公共卫生学院的营养专家和《哈佛健康杂志》（Harvard Health Publications）的编辑共同编制，是规划健康平衡膳食（无论是用餐盘还是餐盒盛装）的指南。在冰箱上张贴该指南，每天提醒您规划健康平衡的膳食！

* **膳食的主要部分应是蔬菜和水果 – 应占据您餐盘的 ½：**

注意蔬菜水果的颜色和品种，并请记住，由于对血糖存在负面影响，马铃薯在“健康饮食餐盘”中不能算作蔬菜。

* **选择全谷食物 – 应占据您餐盘的 ¼：**

全粒完整谷物，包括全麦、大麦、麦仁、藜麦、燕麦、糙米，以及用其制作的食物，例如全麦面食要比白面包、白米和其他细粮对血糖和胰岛素的影响更轻。

This webpage from Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health's The Nutrition Source presents the "Healthy Eating Plate" (健康饮食餐盘) guide in Simplified Chinese. The guide is designed to help plan healthy, balanced meals using a plate or container. The key recommendations are:

1. Fill ½ of your plate with vegetables and fruits (potatoes don't count due to blood sugar impact).
2. Fill ¼ with whole grains (whole wheat, barley, quinoa, oats, brown rice, etc.).
3. Fill ¼ with healthy protein (fish, chicken, beans, nuts; limit red meat, avoid processed meats).
4. Use healthy oils in moderation (olive, canola, soybean, corn, sunflower, peanut oils; avoid partially hydrogenated oils with trans fats).
5. Drink water, coffee, or tea; avoid sugary drinks; limit milk/dairy to 1-2 servings/day and juice to 1 small glass/day.
6. Stay active (symbolized by a red running figure under the plate).

The page emphasizes diet quality over quantity, noting that the type of carbohydrate matters more than the amount, and that healthy oils have no upper calorie limit. It also includes detailed usage terms for reproducing the Healthy Eating Plate image, requiring attribution, non-commercial use, no alterations, and compliance with Harvard's guidelines.

# The Complete List of Healthy Chinese Takeout Options

*For more information on our content creation process, view our [Editorial Policy.](https://www.myorthrive.com/editorial-content-policy)*

## Key Takeaways:

* **Steamed Chicken with Broccoli** ~280–350 calories, lean protein, low fat.
* **Shrimp with Mixed Vegetables (Steamed or Sautéed) –** High in protein, low in carbs and fat.
* **Steamed Vegetable Dumplings –** Lower calorie option for plant-based eaters.
* **Buddha’s Delight (Vegetarian Stir-Fry) –** High in fiber, low in fat, vegan-friendly.
* **Egg Drop Soup (No Added Salt) –** Light starter with ~70–100 calories per cup.

On average, one-third of Americans’ daily calories come from restaurant food ([PMC Study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7443735/)).

Chinese food has cemented its place as a takeout favorite across the United States, no surprise given its range of rich, savory dishes and comforting textures.

In fact, 56% of people who enjoy Chinese food at least a few times per year said they typically order it as takeout or delivery, according to [this industry survey.](https://www.nrn.com/restaurant-segments/survey-consumers-rely-on-restaurants-for-chinese-food)

That number drops to 53% for dining in and just 20% for home cooking, underscoring the central role restaurant offerings play in how Americans consume Chinese cuisine.

At the same time, there’s a growing focus on balanced eating and more thoughtful choices at restaurants, drive-throughs, and delivery apps alike ([source](https://www.myplate.gov/tip-sheet/dine-out-take-out)).

This list will walk you through how to order Chinese takeout that’s just as satisfying as it is nourishing. This way, you can enjoy your favorite dishes while still aligning with your wellness goals.

## Healthy Choices on the Chinese Takeout Menu

Research shows that how your food is prepared matters more than the name of the dish.

Instead of deep-fried or crispy, look for these:

* **Steamed:** This is your lowest-fat option. Dumplings, vegetables, and fish that are steamed skip the added oils and breading.
* **Boiled or Poached:** Often used for soups or tender proteins like shrimp—this method keeps fat content minimal.
* **Baked:** Rare in traditional Chinese dishes, but if available, it’s a solid lean-cooking method.
* **Sautéed:** When done with just a splash of oil and tossed with vegetables and lean meats, sautéed dishes land squarely in the middle, flavorful without extra calories.

[RELATED: McDonald’s Healthy Options](https://myorthrive.com/nutrition/healthy-mcdonald-s-options/)

## Low-Calorie Chinese Takeout Options

Skip the grease and sauce-heavy entrees, and go with steamed chicken and colorful mixed vegetables. This dish offers lean protein, fiber, and essential vitamins while keeping the calorie count in check.

A standard serving of steamed chicken with broccoli contains around [280–350 calories](https://fns-prod.azureedge.us/sites/default/files/resource-files/Broccoli_fresh.pdf), depending on portion size and sauce use. Ask for no or minimal oil, and request brown rice on the side for a whole grain boost.

Choosing steamed, baked, or stir-fried alternatives with minimal sauce instantly cuts calories and fat.

### Master the Sauces: Less Is More

Oyster sauce, hoisin, and General Tso’s glaze can double the calorie count of an otherwise healthy dish.

A smart move? Ask for sauces on the side. This lets you control the quantity and enjoy the dish’s natural flavors. Just one tablespoon of sweet and sour sauce packs around 45–60 calories.

### Low Calories Broth-Based Soups

Before digging into your entrée, warm up with a cup of hot and sour or wonton soup. These soups tend to be low in calories, around 80–100 calories per cup, and help you feel fuller, which may reduce overeating during the meal.

Skip the fried noodles that often come on the side and focus on enjoying the warming broth and soft veggies inside.

## High-Protein, Low Calories Chinese Dishes

Being mindful of your menu choices can help you get more fiber and nutrients while reducing the sodium, sugar, and saturated fat content of your meal ([Source](https://www.myplate.gov/tip-sheet/dine-out-take-out)).

Adjusting your take-out orders to include more nutrient-dense foods can help you reach your health goals.

Protein-packed dishes not only support lean muscle maintenance but also increase satiety, which helps curb overeating. When ordering Chinese takeout, prioritizing high-protein options creates a meal that’s more balanced and satisfying.

Lean cuts of meat, egg-based dishes, and plant-based proteins can all deliver excellent nutrient density without excessive calories.

### Lean and Powerful Proteins Chinese Takeouts

* **Chicken and shrimp stir-fries ([~200–300 cal](https://www.nal.usda.gov/sites/default/files/page-files/Total%20Kcal.pdf)) –** These cook quickly, absorb flavors well, and offer high-quality protein without the fat content associated with red meat. Request light oil or steamed preparations to dial down added calories.
* **Egg-based options like Egg Foo Young –** Packed with eggs and vegetables, Egg Foo Young supplies protein and nutrients in one bite. Opt for sauce on the side to cut sodium. Egg Drop Soup (~70–100 cal per 8 oz), based on [USDA](https://www.nal.usda.gov/sites/default/files/page-files/Total%20Kcal.pdf) broth + egg nutrient values.
* **Tofu stir-fries –** A smart option for vegetarians, tofu is rich in protein and calcium. When combined with broccoli, snow peas, or bok choy, the nutrient profile improves further.

### Protein-Focused Chinese Classic Takeouts

*Szechuan Chicken*

* **Szechuan Chicken –** Lean chicken breast stir-fried with vegetables in a bold, chili-based sauce. Request less oil and sauce to keep it light.
* **Moo Shu Chicken (light sauce) –** A savory mix of shredded chicken, egg, and vegetables. Say no to pancakes and hoisin to keep the dish focused on protein and fiber.
* **Beef with Broccoli –** Tender beef slices and crisp broccoli bathed in garlic sauce. Choose steamed rice over fried and ask for extra vegetables to balance the macros.

### How Protein Shapes Meal Quality

Look at your usual order. Does it rely mostly on rice, fried batter, or sugary sauces?

Swap in grilled chicken, tofu, or egg and focus more on vegetables.

That single shift replaces empty carbs with functional nutrients your body can use to build strength and maintain energy.

## Low-Sodium and Lower-Sugar Chinese Sauces

Sauces drive flavor but can also flood your dish with sodium, sugar, and additives.

In Shanghai, research highlighted that high-sodium condiments and pre‑packaged foods are key drivers of excessive sodium intake, contributing to elevated blood pressure and cardiovascular risk.

Rather than drenching your food in sauce, consider asking for it on the side. Dipping lightly gives you control over how much gets added and how much salt you end up eating.

Want to do even better? Ask your restaurant if they offer a light soy sauce or request a reduced amount during cooking.

*Garlic Sauce*

You don’t have to give up flavour to cut the sugar and salt. Instead of sugary coatings or high-sodium brews, pick sauces that let herbs and aromatics lead:

* **Garlic sauce –** Bold, savory, and typically lower in sugar than sweet sauces.
* **Ginger-scallion –** Fresh and aromatic, often used with steamed proteins.
* **Black bean sauce –** Earthy, deeply flavored, and adds umami with moderate sodium.
* **Light soy sauce –** A gentler alternative to dark sauces; use sparingly.

## Pick Steamed Chinese Takeout Options

Fried foods take a toll on the calorie count. Cooking methods like deep-frying introduce significant amounts of oil, drastically increasing total fat and energy density.

For example, one order of pan-fried pork dumplings (typically 6 pieces) can clock in at around 450–600 calories and 25 grams of fat.

Deep-fried General Tso’s chicken pushes those numbers further, often exceeding 1,300 calories per serving, in part due to battering and sugary sauces.

Why does frying make such a difference?

Foods absorb oil during cooking, and high-heat methods often degrade oils, creating less favorable lipid profiles. That spike in saturated and trans fats outweighs any flavor boost.

Intended as a crispy treat, these items often tip into excess before you’re halfway through your plate.

| Factor | Pan-Fried Dumplings (6 pcs) | Deep-Fried General Tso’s Chicken |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Calories (per serving) | 450–600 kcal | 1,300+ kcal |
| Total Fat | ~25 g | 60–70 g (often) |
| Saturated/Trans Fats | Moderate (depends on oil used) | High (due to oil degradation) |
| Oil Absorption | Lower (shorter contact, less batter) | High (battered, immersed in oil) |
| Cooking Method | Shallow fry, less oil, direct heat | Fully submerged in hot oil |
| Sauce Add-ons | Light soy or dipping sauce | Heavy, sugary sauces |
| Health Risks (Long-term) | Elevated if consumed frequently | Strongly linked to weight gain, heart disease, type 2 diabetes |
| Texture/Flavor Benefit | Crispy, flavorful | Extra crispy, more indulgent |

### Smart Swaps: Dumplings and Stir-Fry Alternatives

* **Steamed dumplings:** Swap pan-fried or deep-fried dumplings for steamed versions. A single steamed pork dumpling contains around 80 calories, compared to nearly 100–120 per fried piece.
* **Try light stir-frying:** True, most stir-fried dishes use oil, but requesting less oil or having your dish stir-fried in broth makes a difference. Szechuan string beans or garlic chicken prepared this way stay flavorful and textural while moderating fat.
* **Skip battered proteins:** Ditch crispy orange beef or sweet and sour chicken that’s deep-fried. Ask for grilled meat or tofu instead and request the sauce on the side.

## Vegetarian and Vegan-Friendly Chinese Meals

Chinese cuisine offers robust vegetarian and vegan-friendly options, many built around tofu, vegetables, mushrooms, and rice or noodles. You won’t need to dig deep on the menu, but you will want to dodge a few common ingredients to keep your dish 100% plant-based and lower in sodium or additives.

### Tofu and Vegetable Stir-Fries That Deliver

*Ma Po Tofu*

* **Ma Po Tofu (sans meat and oyster sauce):** Traditionally served with ground pork and a fermented bean paste, this dish easily becomes vegan when ordered without pork and shellfish-based sauces. Silken tofu brings protein, while the Sichuan peppercorns add a tingling punch.
* **Bok Choy with Garlic:** Crisp baby bok choy, wok-seared and coated in garlic sauce, offers potassium, fiber, and vitamin C. Ask for minimal oil if you’re watching calories.
* **Mixed Vegetable Stir-Fry:** Broccoli, snow peas, water chestnuts, carrots, and mushrooms tossed in a light garlic or brown sauce create a nutrient-dense, colorful plate. Choose steamed tofu for a protein boost without extra fat from frying.

### Chinese Appetizer Options That Don’t Weigh You Down

* **Buddha’s Delight (Lo Han Jai):** A traditional monk’s dish filled with braised tofu, mushrooms, napa cabbage, and glass noodles. It’s light but satisfying, and often steamed or simmered in broth rather than stir-fried.
* **Vegetable Spring Rolls:** Choose those that are steamed or baked instead of deep-fried, if available. They’re usually filled with cabbage, carrots, and bean sprouts—low in calories and high in crunch.

## Simple Swaps That Make Chinese Takeout Instantly Healthier

Many Chinese takeout kitchens are flexible, and a simple request like “less oil, please” can cut hundreds of calories from a single dish.

Don’t forget to mention “no added MSG” if that aligns with your preferences; many places honor it upon request.

### Trade the Fryer for the Steamer or Grill

Crispy Orange Chicken or Sweet and Sour Pork may sound tempting, but those deep-fried coatings come with a heavy load of saturated fat.

Swap battered meats for steamed or grilled alternatives. Steamed chicken with broccoli, garlic shrimp, or grilled tofu stir-fry delivers just as much flavor without the grease.

* **Instead of:** General Tso’s Chicken
* **Try:** Steamed chicken with mixed vegetables
* **Instead of:** Crispy fried beef
* **Try:** Grilled beef with green beans or mushrooms

### Plant-Based Ingredients

Doubling up on vegetables transforms almost any entrée into a fiber-packed meal loaded with antioxidants. You can also substitute tofu for meat without sacrificing protein—firm tofu offers about 10 grams of protein in just half a cup. This small switch supports digestion, heart health, and can help reduce your total calorie intake.

Try asking for dishes like Buddha’s Delight, Ma Po Tofu (with less oil), or vegetable stir-fries, and then add steamed rice or brown rice on the side to round it out.

## Nutritional Highlights of Popular Healthy Chinese Takeout Dishes

| Dish | Calories (kcal) | Protein (g) | Carbs (g) | Fat (g) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Steamed Chicken with Broccoli | 280–350 | 30–35 | 15–20 | 7–10 |
| Shrimp with Mixed Vegetables | 200–300 | 25–30 | 12–18 | 6–8 |
| Egg Drop Soup (1 cup) | 70–100 | 6–7 | 2–3 | 3–4 |
| Buddha’s Delight (Veg Stir-Fry) | 250–350 | 10–15 | 25–35 | 10–15 |
| Steamed Vegetable Dumplings (6 pcs) | 250–300 | 8–10 | 35–40 | 7–10 |

> Values are approximate and may vary depending on preparation method and ingredients used.
>
> Based on [USDA FoodData Central and restaurant nutrition data](https://www.nal.usda.gov/sites/default/files/page-files/Total%20Kcal.pdf)

## FAQs on the Healthiest Chinese Takeouts

### What are the healthiest Chinese takeout dishes to order?

Healthy Chinese takeout options include steamed chicken with broccoli (280–350 calories), shrimp with mixed vegetables, and tofu stir-fries. Choose dishes that are steamed, sautéed with minimal oil, or boiled, and request sauces on the side to control added calories and sodium.

### How can I reduce calories when ordering Chinese food?

Opt for cooking methods like steaming, boiling, or light sautéing, and avoid fried or breaded dishes like General Tso’s chicken. Ask for less oil, no added MSG, and sauces on the side. Swapping fried dumplings for steamed ones can save over 100 calories per serving.

### Which Chinese sauces are lower in sugar and sodium?

Healthier sauce options include garlic sauce, ginger-scallion, black bean sauce, and light soy sauce. These tend to be lower in sugar and sodium compared to hoisin or sweet and sour sauce. Always ask for sauces on the side to moderate your intake.

### Are there vegetarian or vegan-friendly Chinese takeout options?

Yes. Dishes like Buddha’s Delight, Ma Po Tofu (without meat or oyster sauce), bok choy with garlic, and mixed vegetable stir-fries are nutritious and plant-based. Choose steamed or lightly sautéed versions with minimal oil to keep them healthy.

# 7-day Chinese healthy meal plan

This meal plan includes traditional Chinese dishes, as well as some non-traditional options and snacks. It features diabetes-friendly foods, such as low-glycemic-index carbohydrates and healthy fats like canola oil. The carbohydrates are balanced throughout each day with each meal containing 30-45 grams of net carbohydrates, and snacks containing around 15 grams of carbohydrates. Depending on your goals and lifestyle, your calories and carbohydrates may need to be adjusted, so modify the number of snacks or portion sizes accordingly.

## Day 1

**Breakfast:** 1 cup (250 mL) cooked rice vermicelli in soup with shredded chicken and bok choy *(44 g carbohydrates)*

**Lunch:** 9 pieces steamed dumplings and choy sum *(45 g carbohydrates)*

**Dinner:** 1 cup (250 mL) cooked rice, steamed chicken with shiitake mushroom and Chinese cabbage *(45 g carbohydrates)*

## Day 2

**Breakfast:** 1 boiled egg, steamed broccoli and 2 slices multi-grain bread *(30 g carbohydrates)*

**Lunch:** 1 cup (250 mL) cooked rice and steamed chicken with broccoli *(45 g carbohydrates)*

**Dinner:** ⅔ cup (150 mL) cooked rice, pork bone and lotus root soup (1 cup/250 mL lotus root), fish-paste-stuffed tofu, stir-fry celery *(40 g carbohydrates)*

## Day 3

**Breakfast:** Oatmeal made with ⅔ cup/150 mL dry oats with walnuts (tip: add unsweetened ground black sesame or almond for a lower-carbohydrate alternative to sesame soup or almond soup), 1 cup (250 mL) unsweetened calcium-fortified soy beverage *(50 g carbohydrates)*

**Lunch:** 1 whole-wheat steamed vegetable bun and sliced bean curd *(33 g carbohydrates)*

**Dinner:** 1 cup (250 mL) cooked rice, mapo tofu and bok choy *(45 g carbohydrates)*

## Day 4

**Breakfast:** 2 slices multi-grain bread, 1 egg, cucumber, tomato, lettuce, avocado *(30 g carbohydrates)*

**Lunch:** 1½ cups (375 mL) cooked fettuccine\* stir-fry with chicken, carrots, onions and bok choy (\*fettucine is a lower-glycemic-index noodle alternative; cook al dente) *(45 g carbohydrates)*

**Dinner:** 1 cup (250 mL) cooked rice, steamed fish with ginger and green onions and choy sum *(45 g carbohydrates)*

## Day 5

**Breakfast:** Egg and green onion pancake\* wrapped with lettuce and 1 cup (250 mL) unsweetened calcium fortified soy beverage (\*mix 2 eggs, ⅓ cup (75 mL) of flour, green onions cooked with 1 tsp (5 mL) canola oil, and lightly season with salt and pepper) *(35 g carbohydrates)*

**Lunch:** 1½ cups (375 mL) cooked macaroni in soup with mixed vegetables and chicken or beef *(45 g carbohydrates)*

**Dinner:** ⅔ cup (150 mL) cooked rice, steamed pork rib, 1 cup (250 mL) cooked squash and cabbage *(45 g carbohydrates)*

## Day 6

**Breakfast:** 2 cups (500 mL) cooked millet congee, 1 egg, peanuts and blanched leafy vegetables *(45 g carbohydrates)*

**Lunch:** 1½ cups (375 mL) cooked stir-fry noodles with beef/pressed tofu and broccoli *(45 g carbohydrates)*

**Dinner:** ⅔ cup (150 mL) cooked rice, braised chicken with ⅓ cup (75 mL) potatoes and eggplant *(45 g carbohydrates)*

## Day 7

**Breakfast:** 2 cups (500 mL) cooked congee\* with chicken and shredded lettuce (\*tip: Substitute half of rice with oatmeal, mung bean, red bean or barley) *(45 g carbohydrates)*

**Lunch:** tomato and egg with 1½ cups (375 mL) cooked chow mein noodles in soup, garlic-sautéed gai lan *(45 g carbohydrates)*

**Dinner:** ⅔ cup (150 mL) cooked rice, pork shank soup with corn (half of cob) and carrot and stir-fry green beans with minced pork *(45 g carbohydrates)*

---

### Snack Options

Each of the following options provides approximately 15 g carbohydrate and 100–150 calories. If you’re planning to have a snack, consider one of the following choices:

* 1 medium (tennis ball size or 1 cup/250 mL) fruits
* 2% milk or calcium-fortified unsweetened soy milk
* 5 whole-grain crackers, unsalted low-sodium nuts
* 1 slice of multi-grain bread, cheese
* ½ cup (125 mL) plain yogurt with seasonal fruits
* ½ cup (125 mL) shelled edamame

### **Healthy cooking tips**

1. Limit the amount of high-sugar and high-sodium sauces (such as oyster sauce, hoisin sauce, soy sauce).
2. Use low-sodium versions of sauces if available.
3. Try different unsalted herbs for seasonings (including aromatics such as onion or scallions, ginger, garlic, shallots or chili, Szechuan peppercorn, and mushrooms for flavouring stir-fries. Consider Thai basil, coriander, parsley and lemongrass for giving dishes an extra punch of fresh flavour).
4. Mix whole-grains (quinoa, millet, barley, oats, etc.) or beans (such as red bean, mung bean or black bean) into rice or congee to add fibre. Choose whole-grain or brown rice for a higher-fibre option.
5. Consume a moderate amount of healthy dietary fat, such as canola and olive oils.

<webpage_content>
[Skip](#main-content)

# 不是蛋餅、不是地瓜，營養師大推15種最佳「減肥早餐」，「第1種」好吃又健康

By [Women's Health專業編輯群](/tw/author/225373/whtaiwan/ "Women's Health專業編輯群"), Alice Head、Pauline Chen

營養師 Clarissa Lenherr (@clarissalenherrnutrition) 表示：「減重主要是透過消耗比攝取更多的能量來達成，也就是熱量赤字。這並不表示你要吃得很少或只吃低熱量食物，而是要注意零食、份量，以及確保吃進去的食物足夠有飽足感、能持久釋放能量。」

有些人會想乾脆跳過早餐比較有幫助，但專家建議最好別這麼做。根據 美國國家體重控制登記處的資料，吃早餐的人通常比不吃早餐的人體重更輕。美國心臟病學會的研究也指出，跳過早餐可能會導致心臟健康不良。

營養師 Lauren Windas (@laurenwindasnutritionist) 分享：「健康的早餐不僅能為接下來的一天提供適當的營養素，還能讓你有飽足感，避免在兩餐之間忍不住去吃小餅乾墊肚子。」

Windas 建議早餐應該：

## [【別錯過精彩內容】Editors' Choice](/tw/for-you/)

[![Editors' Choice](/_assets/design-tokens/fre/static/icons/user-regular.bdf99d7.svg?primary=%2523000000)登入獲得「個人化推薦」內容](#)

* 熱量相對低（目標約為 400 大卡）
* 高蛋白，能維持更久的飽足感
* 低精緻糖，避免刺激胰島素（一種促進脂肪儲存的荷爾蒙）
* 高纖維，來自植物性碳水化合物，有助於延緩消化

如果你對以上這些目標沒概念，別擔心，我們來幫你。以下精選 15 種最佳健康早餐，每份都控制在 400 大卡以內。這樣加總三餐與一份小點心，一天大約 1500 大卡——這也是 英國國民保健署 (NHS)建議的穩定、持續減重熱量目標，同時也獲得兩位營養師的認可。

這些早餐有什麼特別之處？它們都是營養師精挑細選，不只滿足低熱量需求，還能補充重要的維生素、礦物質、抗氧化物與微量營養素！事不宜遲，趕快看下去吧！

[比168還容易執行的「逆卡路里時間差」飲食法是什麼？「3種人」不適合](https://www.womenshealthmag.com/tw/food-nutrition/diet/g65804265/reverse-calorie-time-gap-diet/)

[營養師推3款「減脂菜單」公開！多加「1物」讓你更快鏟肉無痛超輕鬆](https://www.womenshealthmag.com/tw/food-nutrition/recipes/g35625071/3-chicken-breast-diet-recipe/)

---

## 15 種美味的減重早餐推薦

## 1. 燕麥莓果優格

一碗簡單的希臘優格，加上燕麥與新鮮或冷凍莓果，就是想減肥、又想避免上午 11 點肚子咕嚕叫的理想早餐，營養師 Lenherr 說。

**為什麼它是很棒的減肥早餐？**

優格熱量低、蛋白質高（每 125g 約 60 大卡與 10g 蛋白質），能讓你更持久有飽足感。注意要盡量選擇無糖的希臘優格！

Lenherr 說：「優格富含蛋白質、健康脂肪（如果選擇含活菌的優格，還有益於腸道健康），燕麥提供複合碳水化合物和纖維，莓果則含有大量抗氧化物。」可說是全方位的早餐選擇。

![weight loss breakfast and the best breakfast for weight loss breakfast parfait, overnight oats and greek yogurt in a jar concept of healthy eating, dieting, vegetarian food and tasty breakfast](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/gettyimages-1001971982.jpg?resize=980:* "Weight Loss Breakfast and the Best Breakfast for Weight Loss: Breakfast parfait, overnight oats and greek yogurt in a jar")

Arx0nt

## 2. 奶昔

奶昔常被批評含糖高、甚至熱量高，但如果用對食材，它就是開啟完美早晨的最佳早餐之一！

**為什麼它是很棒的減肥早餐？**

其實奶昔大多數成分其實熱量並不高：水果、蔬菜、牛奶和冰塊，甚至它們讓你能攝取大量維生素與礦物質，卻不會攝入過多熱量。

你可以試試 Lenherr 的完美奶昔公式：「在奶昔裡加入一些健康脂肪（酪梨、堅果醬或椰奶）、蛋白質（蛋白粉、堅果或種子）、低 GI 水果（莓果、蘋果），再搭配大量蔬菜。」

![best weight loss breakfast green smoothie made of spinach,banana,mango in a bowl with blueberry,banana,goji berry and chia seeds topping](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/gettyimages-914856162-1589897933.jpg?resize=980:* "Best Weight Loss Breakfast: Spinach,Banana and Mango Green Smoothie bowl")

vanillaechoes

## 3. 堅果醬黑麥吐司

在黑麥吐司上抹一層堅果醬，再放些莓果，這樣簡單又均衡的早餐就完成了。但要注意別抹太多的花生醬，這樣就不算減重早餐了。

**為什麼它是很棒的減肥早餐？**

Lenherr 說：「黑麥麵包富含纖維與複合碳水，能讓你保持飽足與精力充沛。我會建議在一片黑麥吐司上放一湯匙顆粒堅果醬（隨你喜歡，但務必選無加糖版本才更健康），再撒上一些莓果。」

ax health wins) and some sprinkled berries', shares Lenherr.

![weight loss breakfast sweet delicious gluten free toasts with ripe raspberries, bananas and kiwi](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/gettyimages-641965214-1589898444.jpg?resize=980:* "Weight Loss Breakfast: Toasts with raspberries, bananas and kiwi. Healthy lifestyle")

Zbarovskiy96

## 4. 蔬菜蛋餅

Windas 表示，雞蛋是一種用途超廣的食材，能做出健康又均衡的早餐，Lenherr 也同意。把蔬菜加入蛋餅裡，還能提升膳食纖維攝取。

**為什麼它是很棒的減肥早餐？**

雞蛋熱量低、富含蛋白質與健康脂肪。Windas 說：「一份蔬菜蛋餅能增加蛋白質攝取（一顆蛋約含 6g 蛋白質），讓你更有飽足感，還能輕鬆將富含纖維、維生素、礦物質的低熱量蔬菜納入餐點。」

Lenherr 補充：「蛋黃含有大量有益脂肪與維生素，例如膽鹼和維生素 D。」可說是美味又營養。

![weight loss breakfast omelette with spinach and green peas on wooden background](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/gettyimages-478206386-1589898642.jpg?resize=980:* "Weight Loss Breakfast: omelette with spinach and green peas")

Anna\_Shepulova

## 5. 豆腐蛋餅

豆腐但並其實就像一般蛋餅，但是是素食版。豆腐是一種非常多用途的食材，營養上來說，它是極佳的植物性蛋白質來源，還含有鐵與鈣，以及全部九種必需胺基酸，絕對是全方位選擇。

**為什麼它是很棒的減肥早餐？**

如同蛋餅，豆腐蛋餅同樣能讓你加入滿滿高纖維、維生素和礦物質的蔬菜，同時保持低熱量又美味。

![best breakfasts for weight loss vegan chickpea omelet with broccoli, tomatoes and seedlings on a gray plate healthy vegan food concept](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/gettyimages-1200541837.jpg?resize=980:* "Best Breakfasts for Weight Loss: Vegan chickpea omelet with broccoli, tomatoes and seedlings, top view. Healthy vegan food concept.")

vaaseenaa

## 6. 早餐馬芬

不是常見的那種巧克力馬芬，而是另一種把雞蛋融入早餐的多變做法。

**為什麼它是很棒的減肥早餐？**

Windas 說：「同樣地，雞蛋熱量低、營養密度高。早餐馬芬質地輕盈蓬鬆，搭配蔬菜和香草烘焙後非常美味。配上一份綠葉沙拉，就是低熱量又能滿足味蕾的早餐，讓你一整天心情愉快。」

她最喜歡的口味是風乾番茄和細香蔥。

~mediaId='1207f384-272e-484e-89c3-3b3145893a5f' align='center' size='large' share='false' caption='' expand='' crop='original'][/image]

## 7. 素食馬芬

馬芬完全可以不用雞蛋來做，同樣能成為美味的低熱量早餐，非常適合想減掉幾公斤的你！有好幾種植物性食材替代方案，你可以用鷹嘴豆罐頭裡的液體（Aquafaba，烘焙時能替代蛋白），或試試加入種子或營養酵母來取代。

**為什麼它是很棒的減肥早餐？**

視乎你加入的食材，素食馬芬通常會含有低熱量、營養密度高的蔬菜，以及富含健康脂肪和纖維的種子。絕對是健康又美味可口。

![breakfasts for weight loss vegan breakfast muffins](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/savoury-muffins-5-1591088710.jpg?resize=980:* "Breakfasts for Weight Loss: Spinach and Tomato Vegan Muffins")

The Vegan Larder

## 8. 燕麥粥

經典中的經典，營養界對燕麥粥的喜愛可不是沒有原因的。

**為什麼它是很棒的減肥早餐？**

只要注意份量、別在配料上放太多花樣，燕麥粥就能提供高含量的慢釋放碳水化合物、纖維，且熱量低（45g 燕麥約 150 大卡）。

想要點變化嗎？Windas 說：「藜麥是極佳的植物性蛋白質來源（對素食者尤其好，因為它含有所有必需胺基酸），也是燕麥粥的好替代品，能替餐桌帶來多樣性。上面加上莓果補充維生素 C，再抓一把杏仁提供健康的單元不飽和脂肪。」

![weight loss breakfasts bowl of homemade oatmeal porridge with banana, blueberries, almonds, coconut and caramel sauce on teal rustic table from above, hot and healthy food for breakfast](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/gettyimages-546787366-1589899695.jpg?resize=980:* "Weight Loss Breakfasts: Bowl of homemade oatmeal porridge with banana, blueberries and almonds")

Julia\_Sudnitskaya

## 9. 番茄烘蛋

準備好迎接 Windas 所說的「美妙的鹹味蛋料理」了嗎？它也完全適合減重餐單。

為什麼它是好的減脂早餐？

Windas 解釋：「這道菜碳水化合物含量低、蛋白質含量高，能讓你一路飽到午餐時間。」再加點綠葉蔬菜，營養更上一層樓。

![weight loss breakfast green shakshuka in a cast iron pan on a grey slate,stone or concrete backgroundtop view](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/gettyimages-694477824-1589899867.jpg?resize=980:* "Weight Loss Breakfast: Green shakshuka in a cast iron pan")

Lilechka75

## 10. 奇亞籽布丁

聽過奇亞籽布丁嗎？其實超簡單！只要把奇亞籽浸泡在你選擇的牛奶裡，放進冰箱一晚就完成了。

**為什麼它是很棒的減肥早餐？**

Windas 說：「奇亞籽富含纖維、維生素與礦物質、Omega-3 脂肪酸，還是完整蛋白質來源。」Lenherr 也同意，但他也提醒如果你在減重，要注意份量，因為奇亞籽的脂肪含量也不低。

![weight loss breakfast chia seed pudding with persimmon in glass concept of healthy lifestyle, healthy eating, dieting, weight loss and balanced meal diet](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/gettyimages-916423154-1589900631.jpg?resize=980:* "Weight Loss Breakfast: Chia seed pudding with persimmon in glass")

Arx0nt

## 11. 炒豆腐吐司

素食者有福了！植物性飲食也有很多減重早餐選擇。炒豆腐配吐司，就是一種簡單又美味的開始一天的方式（而且熱量可控）。

**為什麼它是很棒的減肥早餐？**

Windas 說：「豆腐是優秀的蛋白質來源，可以抑制飢餓感，這道料理也是炒蛋的理想替代品。」而且一份炒豆腐配上全麥籽類吐司大約 360 大卡，完全符合每餐控制在 400 大卡以下的建議。

![weight loss breakfast tofu scrambled eggs with sun dried tomatoes  spinach and tomato  cucumber salad, with bread](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/gettyimages-1151535671.jpg?resize=980:* "Weight Loss Breakfast: Tofu scrambled eggs with sun dried tomatoes & spinach and tomato & cucumber salad, with bread")

Bartosz Luczak

## 12. 鬆餅

鬆餅？在減重期間也能吃？沒錯！你可以嘗試多種變化（例如香蕉鬆餅、蕎麥鬆餅、高蛋白鬆餅？）。只要保持在 400 大卡以下、不含大量精製糖，並且用新鮮食材在家裡製作，鬆餅也能是營養豐富的早餐選擇。

**為什麼它是很棒的減肥早餐？**

取決於食材，鬆餅可以富含纖維、維生素和礦物質。Windas 說：「我喜歡蘋果香蕉蕎麥鬆餅，搭配莓果。」它們不含麩質與乳製品，是週末早餐的好選擇，既能平衡營養，又能滿足想吃甜點的心。

![weight loss breakfast close up of delicious pancakes with fresh fruits, berries and maple syrup on a plate](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/gettyimages-921436884-1589901291.jpg?resize=980:* "Weight Loss Breakfast: Close-up of delicious pancakes with fresh fruits, berries and maple syrup on a plate")

Alexander Spatari

## 13. 煙燻鮭魚蛋吐司

這是一個營養與美味兼具，非常全方位的早餐組合。

**為什麼它是很棒的減肥早餐？**

Windas 解釋：「煙燻鮭魚富含蛋白質與 Omega-3 脂肪酸，是早餐的絕佳選擇，特別是搭配水波蛋流心蛋黃和一片黑麥吐司時，更是美味又營養。」

![weight loss breakfast rye bread with smashed avocado, smoked salmon and poached egg with yolk flow](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/gettyimages-945223540-1589901480.jpg?resize=980:* "Weight Loss Breakfast: Bread with avocado, smoked salmon and poached egg yolk flowing")

Pink-Orange-Photography

## 14. 蛋白燕麥粥

試過「Proats」嗎？（就是「Protein + Oats」的縮寫）。如果還沒試過，Windas 說你真的錯過了。「將蛋白粉與燕麥粥結合，就是最美味又健康的早餐。」

**為什麼它是很棒的減肥早餐？**

顧名思義，蛋白質含量高、含有慢釋放碳水，熱量不高，能幫助你走在減重的正確軌道上。Windas 補充：「搭配香蕉片、枸杞和奇亞籽，能讓風味更佳，也提升營養密度。」

![weight loss breakfast organic breakfast quinoa with nuts milk and berries](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/gettyimages-534107155-1589901718.jpg?resize=980:* "Weight Loss Breakfast: Organic Breakfast Quinoa with Nuts")

bhofack2

## 15. 素食蛋白燕麥粥

基本上和蛋白燕麥粥一樣，只是不加乳清蛋白，選擇植物性蛋白粉加入早晨或隔夜燕麥，就能得到一份適合素食者的高蛋白早餐，而且方便攜帶，無論在家或外出都能享用。

**為什麼它是很棒的減肥早餐？**
